primary_claim: A random forest trained on ADELE's cognitive-demand dimensions outperforms a finetuned LLaMA-3.1-8B on out-of-distribution calibration (ECE 0.022 vs 0.075) and marginally on out-of-distribution discrimination (AUROC), while also yielding human-interpretable explanations of task/system profiles.

effect.value: ECE 0.022 (demand-based random forest) vs 0.075 (finetuned LLaMA-3.1-8B) out-of-distribution; AUROC only marginally better for the random forest, though statistically significant

contradicts_or_qualifies: Contrasts with factor-analysis approaches to capability dimensions (Burnell et al 2023; Ruan et al 2024), which find uncorrelated dimensions but whose results are only valid for the specific population of tested models and data and are less interpretable
stated_future_work: Improve calibration of the demand scales against human populations
Extend the demand scales to higher levels of difficulty to address benchmark saturation
Extend the methodology from capabilities to propensities (e.g. deception, goal-directedness)
Add missing capabilities such as agentic planning/execution and self-control
Develop 'assessor' meta-AI systems that use the methodology to predict/assess situation safety
limitations_stated: 18 dimensions may look like an overabundance even though hierarchically structured
The AUROC improvement over a finetuned LLM is modest
Limited AUROC gains may reflect a lack of sufficiently challenging instances across most dimensions in the current ADELE battery v1.0
As with any evaluation method, it could speed up AI capability development by revealing which capabilities are most fundamental
quote: A random forest trained on task demands and instance performance outperforms a finetuned LLaMA-3.1-8B on discrimination (AUROC) out of distribution, and calibration (Expected Calibration Error) in-distribution and out-of-distribution
